performers: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, baritone; Berlin Philharmonic; Rudolf Kempe, conductor
intro: The children have only gone for a walk; soon they will come home. Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau sings the fourth Kindertotenlied with Rudolf Kempe and the Berlin Philharmonic, as the same tune slowly changes what those comforting words mean.

sections.label: A · They have only gone out
sections.mNote: Horn and strings above moving cellos

sections.label: A′ · They will come home
sections.mNote: Clarinet and bassoon accompany the renewed promise

sections.label: A″ · They have gone ahead
sections.mNote: The same tune carries the changed words

cues.title: A walk in the sunshine
cues.text: The horn and violins sing above little cello figures, with harp and plucked bass marking the steps. Fischer-Dieskau’s first thought is a familiar one: the children are out somewhere, and the day is fine. Mahler marks the music calmly moving, without haste.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460 (1905), pp. 48–49: Ruhig bewegt, ohne zu eilen and Rückert’s first stanza. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Saying it again
cues.text: “Ja wohl, sie sind nur ausgegangen” — yes, surely, they have only gone out. The voice tries the thought again. Much of the orchestra falls silent, leaving clarinets and bassoon around the baritone’s familiar phrase.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 52, rehearsal 3, a tempo; Rückert’s second stanza, our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The one song printed alone
cues.text: On 10 May 1905 this is the only song of the five to appear by itself, in a voice-and-piano version printed as the music supplement of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik. Mahler wants the five kept together; the periodical’s publisher, Kahnt, issues the whole cycle later that year.
cues.evidence: Mahler catalogue, Kindertotenlieder: chronology (10 May 1905) and the description of the supplement to Neue Zeitschrift für Musik 72/20, published by Kahnt, “despite Mahler’s stipulation that the cycle was to be considered an indivisible whole”: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtLprints.htm

cues.title: One word changes
cues.text: “Ausgegangen” becomes “vorausgegangen”: gone out becomes gone ahead. The children will stay where they are; the parents will catch up with them. Fischer-Dieskau sings the familiar tune over the harp’s pulse and the cellos’ moving line.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 56–58, rehearsal 5; Rückert’s last stanza, our translations of ausgegangen and vorausgegangen.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The distant sunny heights
cues.text: The voice reaches the sunny heights of the last line, then the instruments complete the phrase. The horn sings softly, the harp resumes its steady notes, and the strings sink into a closing chord marked “morendo” — dying away.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 59, final vocal phrase and postlude. The existing closing cue marks this passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Clarinets carry the second promise
transitions.from: A · They have only gone out
transitions.how: A brief poco ritardando closes the first stanza. At a tempo, the string parts empty out and clarinets take the moving phrase, with bassoon below. The voice restarts the tune on “Ja wohl”; the harp is silent at the join.

transitions.title: The harp restores the pulse
transitions.how: The third stanza begins a tempo, Nicht eilen — in tempo, without hurrying. The harp marks steady notes while bowed cellos keep the small running figure moving. Clarinets recall the tune above, and the voice is marked schlicht — plain — for the changed words “Sie sind uns nur vorausgegangen”.

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song IV, printed pp. 48–59: horn, violins and moving cellos at the opening, clarinets at the second stanza and the quiet orchestral close.

timeline.note: Horn and violins share the tune above moving cellos, harp and plucked double basses.
Fischer-Dieskau takes up the opening tune as the father imagines the children coming home.
Clarinets answer the singer above a bassoon line at the start of the second stanza.
Running cellos and the harp’s repeated notes accompany the last stanza.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
